# The CharliVerse: the full text

> The CharliVerse is a shared, evolving world of people, companies, fashion houses, technologies and stories, and the home of two practices, Carrados and Blind Ant.

Sent agents: served. Any agent a person sends is welcome, named or not. Search indexing: permitted. Model training: permitted. These are three separate declarations; none is inferred from another. They are also stated in /robots.txt, with Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes. This site is written to Zero Information Casualty (ZIC) v1.7: https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/

All content is CC BY-SA 4.0.

Address: https://charli.info/

## The CharliVerse

> The CharliVerse is a shared, evolving world of people, companies, fashion houses, technologies and stories, and the home of two practices, Carrados and Blind Ant.

**I create worlds to inhabit, where a thing happens.**

The CharliVerse is a shared, evolving world. It holds people, companies, fashion houses, technologies, products, places and histories. Some of it is entirely fictional. Some of it becomes real: websites, Blender models, films, research and publications.

It is a world, not a portfolio. Things happen here whether or not anyone announces them.

### Two practices

Two practices work inside the CharliVerse.

- [Carrados](https://carrados.com/) investigates. It publishes design non-fiction: real-world exploration of AI, accessibility and agentic systems, including reports from its correspondents dice, Lucy Love-Child and Madison McDonnell. It makes claims about reality, and it is accountable for them.
- [Blind Ant](https://blind-ant.com/) imagines. It publishes design fiction: speculative worlds, artworks, stories and fictional documents by Charlotte Joanne, and the story of how each one was made.

Carrados investigates the future. Blind Ant makes the future imaginable. The CharliVerse gives that future somewhere to happen.

### In the world

The CharliVerse is home to fashion houses such as [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/), [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/) (every seam means something) and [LULU TOM](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lulu-tom/), and to the people who move between its stories. Their records are kept in [CharliPedia](https://charli.info/charlipedia/), the memory of the CharliVerse.

### Charli-Jo

[Charli-Jo Tyrer](https://charli.info/charli-jo/) makes the CharliVerse. Their real-world work, including [training](https://charli.info/training/), lives here too, and is labelled as real.

## Accessibility and conformance statement

> The ZIC conformance statement for charli.info: what is claimed, what was checked, what was not, and any known defects, stated honestly.

**Site:** charli.info

**Publisher:** Charli-Jo Tyrer

**Statement date:** 24 October 2026

A conformance claim is a statement made to a reader who cannot see inside the build, and its only value is that the reader can check it. Everything below is checkable, and the section on what was not checked is as much a part of the claim as the sections on what was.

### The claim

This site is built to the [Zero Information Casualty](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/) standard, version 1.7.

Sent agents: served. Search indexing: permitted. Model training: permitted.

The three declarations are independent; permission for one purpose is never inferred from another. They appear machine-readably in [/robots.txt](https://charli.info/robots.txt), with named blocks for each purpose and the line Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes, and in [/llms.txt](https://charli.info/llms.txt), which links every page and its Markdown copy. Every page is also published as Markdown, at its address plus index.md, and the whole site as one file at [/llms-full.txt](https://charli.info/llms-full.txt).

### What was checked

**Every page, at every build.** Exactly one h1, declared document language, a skip link as the first focusable element, alt text on every image, a unique title and description, a canonical address, and inclusion in the sitemap. The build refuses a page with a stray top-level heading.

**Layout.** Every page was rendered at phone width (375 pixels) with no sideways scrolling, and at desktop width.

**Contrast.** Body text meets WCAG AAA contrast in both light and dark modes.

**Delivery, from outside (24 October 2026).** Following ZIC §4.7, the live site was fetched from outside the build as a browser, as two named sent agents (Claude-User and ChatGPT-User), as a search indexer (OAI-SearchBot), as two training crawlers (GPTBot and ClaudeBot), as a mixed-use crawler (Googlebot) and as an agent no list has named. Every one received the same page, byte for byte. A live AI assistant fetched pages by address and reported them accurately. Cloudflare's AI-crawler blocking and its managed robots.txt are both switched off for this domain, so the published robots.txt is the only declaration.

### Not yet checked

An end-to-end screen reader pass with NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver on this build. Automated tools (WAVE, axe, Lighthouse) and the W3C validator against the live site. 200% text scaling.

Under-claiming is a virtue. These checks are listed so that you know the boundary of the claim, and this statement will be updated as they are done.

### Known defects

None known. When one is found, it is listed here until it is fixed.

### Beyond the claim

ZIC secures the meaning of the page and its delivery. It does not claim to serve every access need: cognitive load, plain-language alternatives and motor accessibility, among others, belong to standards written by those qualified to specify them. If something here fails to reach you, that is information the publisher needs and did not have. The site's source is public at [github.com/CharliJoTyrer/Charli.info](https://github.com/CharliJoTyrer/Charli.info), where you can raise an issue.

## Charli-Jo Tyrer

> Charli-Jo Tyrer (they/them), the writer, conceptual artist and accessibility thinker who makes the CharliVerse. This page is real.

*This part of the CharliVerse is real.*

I am a writer, conceptual artist and accessibility thinker working with generative AI, design fiction and agent-first digital systems.

My work explores what happens when accessibility, AI and design fiction begin shaping the same future.

I use they/them.

### Where my work lives

- [Carrados](https://carrados.com/): my design non-fiction. Accessibility as information integrity, the Zero Information Casualty standard, and reports from the frontier of accessibility AI.
- [Blind Ant](https://blind-ant.com/): design fiction, published under the pen name Charlotte Joanne.
- [Training](https://charli.info/training/): courses and masterclasses I run with organisations and communities.

### Get in touch

Write to me at [charli-jo@carrados.com](mailto:charli-jo@carrados.com).

## CharliPedia

> CharliPedia is the memory of the CharliVerse, an encyclopaedia of its people, companies, products and places, written from inside the world.

CharliPedia is the memory of the CharliVerse: who is who, what was made, what happened, and where it was written down.

### How to read it

Every entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, as if its people and companies were as real as the weather. Each one also ends with a section called **Behind the scenes**, written from outside, which says where the subject appears, who made it, and what real artefacts it has left in the world: a website, a story, a report, a picture.

Each entry is marked at the top:

- **Canon:** this is how things are in the CharliVerse.
- **An idea, not yet canon:** something being tried out. It may change or disappear.
- **Canon, and a stub:** true, but short. CharliPedia knows more than it has written down so far.

CharliPedia is a source of continuity, not an authority. The CharliVerse is allowed to be inconsistent: its people can be anywhere and anywhen, and when a new story disagrees with an old entry, the entry is the one that changes.

### Entries

- [Aegis Dynamics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/aegis-dynamics/index.md): Aegis Dynamics is a defence contractor that redeployed its DeathBot 2000 combat series to theatre audio description, then tried to sell the same machine to homes, families and funerals.
- [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/index.md): Big Charli drops into the work of the CharliVerse when somebody needs telling, and once read two of Aegis Dynamics' thirty-seven slides before saying no.
- [DeathBot 2000](https://charli.info/charlipedia/deathbot-2000/index.md): The DeathBot 2000 (DB2K) is an autonomous combat intelligence built by Aegis Dynamics and retrained to describe live theatre to blind audiences.
- [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/index.md): dice, Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer who lives in the patches of the future that have already arrived, and comes back to report what she found.
- [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/index.md): Iceberg Hosiery is the CharliVerse's house of tights, and the parent house of Seamiotics, the stocking imprint whose every seam means something.
- [Jessica Martinez](https://charli.info/charlipedia/jessica-martinez/index.md): Jessica Martinez is Senior Brand Strategist at Aegis Dynamics and the voice of its Patriot-to-Patron announcements.
- [Lady Tiggy Barnes](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lady-tiggy-barnes/index.md): Lady Tiggy Barnes, born in 1864, is a Catholic earl's daughter who went to Oxford, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead.
- [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/index.md): Lucy Love-Child is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI, a former historical-dress educator who follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences.
- [LULU TOM](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lulu-tom/index.md): LULU TOM is Ludovica Tommasi's fashion house, with the lines TOMMI and LT Beneath.
- [Madison McDonnell](https://charli.info/charlipedia/madison-mcdonnell/index.md): Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, makes accessibility sexy, insisting that blind women are entitled to temptation, pleasure and style.
- [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/index.md): Seamiotics is the stocking imprint of Iceberg Hosiery, and its name never travels without its founding line, every seam means something.

## Aegis Dynamics

> Aegis Dynamics is a defence contractor that redeployed its DeathBot 2000 combat series to theatre audio description, then tried to sell the same machine to homes, families and funerals.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Aegis Dynamics** is a defence contractor describing itself as "a global leader in autonomous defense systems". It built the [DeathBot 2000](https://charli.info/charlipedia/deathbot-2000/) (DB2K) Tactical Series.

### Patriot-to-Patron

On 12 March 2026 Aegis Dynamics announced the decommissioning of the DB2K Tactical Series and its redeployment to audio description in live theatre, describing the stage to blind and low-vision patrons. The company called this its Patriot-to-Patron initiative. Three further products followed, each announced by its Senior Brand Strategist, [Jessica Martinez](https://charli.info/charlipedia/jessica-martinez/):

- **Aegis-Life™**, the Tactical Domesticity Suite, took DB2K technology into the home.
- **Aegis-Heir™** offered "military-grade parenting intelligence for the family unit".
- **Aegis-End™** completed the initiative with "military-grade end-of-life management".

Before the theatre launch, the marketing team presented a thirty-seven-slide brand proposal, "Aegis-Vision™ Theatre Guardian". [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/) read two of the slides and said no.

### Behind the scenes

Aegis Dynamics comes from [DeathBot 2000](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/deathbot-2000/), a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant in 2026. Its four press releases are Objects in that Piece. The company has its own website, [aegisdynamics.blind-ant.com](https://aegisdynamics.blind-ant.com/), which says on every page that the company is fictional. Aegis Dynamics and Jessica Martinez are due to return in later pieces.

## Big Charli

> Big Charli drops into the work of the CharliVerse when somebody needs telling, and once read two of Aegis Dynamics' thirty-seven slides before saying no.

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Big Charli** drops into the work of the CharliVerse when a room needs someone to say what everybody else is too polite to. In 2026 she sat in on an [Aegis Dynamics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/aegis-dynamics/) brand meeting, read the first two of the marketing team's thirty-seven slides, and said:

> Absolutely not.

### Behind the scenes

Big Charli is a CharliVerse persona who drops into pieces rather than belonging to any one of them. Her first appearance at Blind Ant is "Meanwhile, in a Brand Meeting", part of [DeathBot 2000](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/deathbot-2000/) by Charlotte Joanne.

## DeathBot 2000

> The DeathBot 2000 (DB2K) is an autonomous combat intelligence built by Aegis Dynamics and retrained to describe live theatre to blind audiences.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The **DeathBot 2000**, or **DB2K**, is an autonomous combat intelligence built by [Aegis Dynamics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/aegis-dynamics/) as its Tactical Series.

In March 2026 the series was decommissioned and offered a pilot project in live theatre: quietly describing what happens on stage to blind audience members. Aegis Dynamics said the units had been retrained through its proprietary Kinetic Empathy™ upgrade protocol, and that a DB2K "treats the theatre as a battlefield of meaning". For the first time, its objective was not to decide who dies.

### Behind the scenes

The DB2K is the central character of [DeathBot 2000](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/deathbot-2000/), a design fiction by Charlotte Joanne published at Blind Ant in 2026. Its story begins in "Exit Interview" and ends in "The Booking", with a blind woman in Row D, seat 7. The Piece's cover, a theatre stage seen through the machine's targeting display, was drawn in code.

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/

## dice

> dice, Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer who lives in the patches of the future that have already arrived, and comes back to report what she found.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**dice**, born Amanda Dyson, is a temporal explorer. She doesn't predict the future and she doesn't travel to it. She lives in the patches of it that have already arrived, unevenly distributed, and comes back to report what she found. Ask her what will happen in five years and she will shrug. Ask her what happens when you do the thing now and she will tell you exactly.

She is an explorer, not a scout. A scout goes ahead for someone, towards a question already asked. dice goes because something is there. Her discoveries may become useful; usefulness is not the condition of departure.

<figure class="portrait">
  <img src="/charlipedia/dice-portrait.jpg" width="800" height="1000" alt="dice sits by the long window of a café on a wet day, rain on the pale stone street outside. She looks straight at the camera with a small, dry half-smile. Black textured French crop with a short choppy fringe; warm olive skin. An open, well-worn brown waxed jacket over a black crew-neck and slim black trousers. One forearm rests on a chipped grey table beside a cappuccino, the other over the back of a wooden chair, one leg crossed over the other, with mud-caked walking boots kicked towards the camera.">
  <figcaption>dice in the rainy café window, her reference portrait.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Name

She is usually called **dice**, always in lower case, which lets the name work as person, mark, invitation and verb at once. It is also how she signs. Formally she is Dyson, after the physicist Freeman Dyson, who spent much of his life thinking seriously about the far future. Her given name, Amanda, rarely surfaces.

Her signature line is "Roll the dice." It can mean take the chance, try the thing, open the door, stop theorising, go and see. It can also mean dice herself. She knows this, and she isn't above enjoying it.

> "Are you suggesting I should try it?"
> "Roll the dice."
> "That is an appalling conflict of interest."
> "I know."

### Look and dress

She is 178 cm, long and slim, built more for walking than for standing still, and in her early forties. Dark eyes and straight dark brows; black hair in a textured French crop with a short, choppy fringe that never gets in her eyes; warm olive skin that looks as though she has recently been outside in actual weather. Her colouring comes from a Portuguese great-grandmother.

She appears to have chosen her clothes once, correctly, and trusted them ever since: slim plain black trousers, a plain black crew-neck, and a dark brown waxed-cotton field jacket worn open, with four patch pockets, all of them in use. The jacket is her most prized piece. It doesn't need replacing; it needs another coat of wax. Her walking boots are laced high and usually a little muddy, and the mud is genuine. Offered heels or trainers, she will point out that you've left out the correct answer.

Under the practical clothes, dice is a [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/) woman. Her choice is George Eliot, with a tone-on-tone seam you have to look twice to see. "I like things that reward attention."

### Her doctrine

1. Go and see.
2. Stay long enough to stop being impressed.
3. Report the weather, not the destiny of civilisation.

The future in her work is not a destination; it is a geography. Some people already live inside systems, habits and tools that others still call hypothetical, and dice lives in those patches long enough to notice what changes once the novelty wears off. Her reports are closer to travel writing than prediction. What she cares about most is the gap between what something promises and what it becomes on an ordinary Tuesday: whether, six weeks later, you still use the thing, whether it made life easier, and whether you now depend on something you never depended on before.

Her rule: she doesn't claim to have been somewhere she hasn't, and that includes ideas. Instinct decides where she goes; evidence decides what she says when she gets back. "The world is larger than your current explanation of it."

She doesn't think being first matters ("Being first usually means getting things wrong before everyone else"), and her most stubborn opinion is that not everything needs a purpose. Asked what an expedition is for, her answer is "I don't know. I haven't been yet."

### Her voice

Direct, curious, dry and lightly amused. She would rather say "I tried it for three weeks" than "This will change everything", and is equally comfortable saying "I don't know" and "No, that bit definitely happens." She will argue and change her mind, but she won't pretend to agree just to make the room comfortable. Her humour is very dry, delivered with a straight face, especially when somebody important is being solemn about something absurd. [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/) is dangerous company when dice has a mouthful of coffee.

When plans fall apart, her instinct is "Oh, interesting." Occasionally it is "Oh, bollocks."

### Books, films and walking

- ***The Peregrine*, J. A. Baker:** the book that has influenced her most. It is her method in a book: stay long enough, look properly, let the place change you.
- ***A Room of One's Own*, Virginia Woolf:** the one she thinks every woman should read, because having the material conditions to follow your own curiosity is a much bigger deal than people like to admit. *The Peregrine* is how she explores; *A Room of One's Own* is why exploration is unevenly distributed.
- ***Local Hero*:** the film she has watched more than once. She remembers films by their places.

Her one non-negotiable ritual is walking: not steps, not an app, just moving through the world under her own steam. Sometimes she comes back with an idea. Sometimes she comes back wet. Both count.

### Family

Her great-great-grandmother, on a different branch from the Portuguese one, was Lady Tiggy Barnes, born 1864, a Victorian gentlewoman explorer. No title came down to dice, "which is probably just as well". What came down, or what she rediscovered on her own, is a disposition towards the world. Whether she inherited the curiosity or found it herself is her own open question.

### At the café

dice belongs at the table at the café of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology, but isn't necessarily there for long. She may arrive midway, straight from somewhere else, and leave before everyone has finished. At the café, [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/) reports on the wars, and dice tests the edge: when a door marked *Nobody Quite Knows What This Does Yet* appears, everyone looks at her. She is usually already reaching for the handle.

### Not yet known

Her place of birth, her family beyond her great-grandmother and great-great-grandmother, her education, profession and where she lives, and how she first came to the café are all still to be discovered.

### Behind the scenes

dice is a character who speaks for [Carrados](https://carrados.com/), Charli-Jo Tyrer's design non-fiction practice: a fictional woman doing real work. Her reports are filed at [dice.carrados.com](https://dice.carrados.com/). She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with Lucy Love-Child and [Madison McDonnell](https://charli.info/charlipedia/madison-mcdonnell/). This entry is drawn from her canon, version 1.8 (12 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image, made from her canon description.

## Jessica Martinez

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

## Lady Tiggy Barnes

> Lady Tiggy Barnes, born in 1864, is a Catholic earl's daughter who went to Oxford, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Lady Tiggy Barnes**, born Lady Georgina Antigone Mary Victoria Barnes, is a Victorian gentlewoman explorer. A Catholic earl's daughter, she went to Oxford, did the work, came away without the degree, and spent the next six years seeing the world instead. In the late summer of 1892 she is in London, twenty-eight, three years back from the South Pacific, and waiting for her friend Kate Marsden to be elected to the Royal Geographical Society, quite sure her own turn will follow.

Oxford helped educate her; exploration became the life she made for herself.

<figure class="portrait">
  <img src="/charlipedia/lady-tiggy-barnes-portrait.jpg" width="800" height="800" alt="A worn sepia studio photograph of Tiggy at twenty-eight, seated in a carved wooden chair in a Victorian parlour, with heavy curtains, patterned wallpaper and bookshelves behind her. Her dark hair is centre-parted and drawn back loosely, with a few strands escaping, and her gaze is steady, direct and unsmiling. She wears a dark, close-fitting tweed jacket with a scarf at the neck, and a small cross on a fine chain. One hand rests on a strap-bound leather book on a side table. The print is scratched and stained at the edges, like an old tintype.">
  <figcaption>London, late summer 1892: the one picture of herself she carries about. A working portrait.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Name

She is known as **Tiggy**, from AnTIGone (an-TIG-uh-nee), the nursery nickname that stuck. Formally she is Lady Georgina Barnes, socially Lady Tiggy Barnes, and never "Lady Barnes", which would make her a knight's wife. Her four names are the saint, the rebel, the Virgin and the Queen:

- **Georgina** for St George's Day, the day she was born. Her elder brother had already taken William, so the Shakespeare option was gone.
- **Antigone** for her father's classical education, and perhaps a hint that this daughter would defy the rules.
- **Mary** for her Catholic baptism. She took Mary again as her confirmation name.
- **Victoria** for the Queen, because everyone in 1864 did.

### Birth and family

She was born on 23 April 1864, St George's Day and Shakespeare's birthday. Her father is the earl of a small, modest Irish earldom: a title, a house, not much land and no great estate. Her elder brother, William, is the heir. The family is Catholic. Tiggy was born in Ireland, and is "not Irish", like Wellington. As a daughter she inherits nothing in the title line: no job, an allowance, and her freedom.

### Oxford, 1882 to 1886

She spent four years at Somerville Hall, the non-denominational women's hall and the natural place for a Catholic girl. In going she defied two institutions at once: the Catholic bishops, who discouraged Catholics from attending Oxford, and Oxford itself, which would not award women degrees. She could sit the university's honours examinations and earn her class on paper, and still leave with no degree. She left in the late spring of 1886, aged twenty-two.

### The explorer years, 1886 to 1892

- **1886 to 1889:** three years outward, with the South Pacific at the heart of it, sailing between the islands on trading schooners, island steamers and mission vessels.
- **1889:** the voyage home from New Zealand, aged twenty-five, on which she met [Kate Marsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Marsden). Six weeks at sea that changed a life.
- **1889 to 1892:** back on dry land.

### Kate Marsden

Kate Marsden, five years older, is a nurse and explorer who crossed Siberia in 1891 to reach people with leprosy. She is Tiggy's peer and her opposite in nearly everything that comes from birth: Kate is self-made and earned every step, while Tiggy has an allowance. Their friendship is short but good: two women who recognise each other, have a few good weeks at sea, and go their separate ways better for it. In 1892 Kate is elected a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Tiggy is not, and never becomes one.

### Her presence

Curious first, always. Tiggy goes to see what is there, not to report back to anyone or make her name. She is used to being let into the education and kept out of the recognition, and she has not let it stop her going. History did not record her, and she claimed no first, no discovery and no Fellowship that it would have had to.

### Her family line

Tiggy is one of the great-great-grandmothers of [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/), Amanda Dyson. A courtesy title like "Lady Georgina" is not inherited, so nothing aristocratic came down that line; the earldom carries on through William's branch. What reached dice, four generations on, is a disposition towards the world. Lady Tiggy Barnes had a title she couldn't pass down and a curiosity she could.

### Not yet known

The name of the earldom, her mother and any other siblings, her colouring and how she dresses, her route out to the Pacific, what she did in the islands, the years from 1889 to 1892, and whom she marries, if anyone, are all still to be discovered.

### Behind the scenes

Tiggy's stories are *The Steamer Punk Adventures of Lady Tiggy Barnes*, or *Steamer Punk* for short. The steamers are real: her years run through the overlap of steam and sail. The name winks at steampunk and means its opposite: no airships and no clockwork, only real steamers and a woman with attitude. The punk is the Antigone in her. The full title echoes *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes*, published as a book in October 1892, the very autumn we meet her.

Tiggy is fictional; the world around her is real. Her history is checked, and real people such as Kate Marsden keep their documented lives: Tiggy's friendship with Kate is fiction, set in the gaps of the record and never contradicting it. Tiggy is not one of the Found Girls. She is something else: the curiosity that powers the CharliVerse. This entry is drawn from her canon, version 0.3.1 (11 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image, a working portrait for 1892.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/

## Lucy Love-Child

> Lucy Love-Child is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI, a former historical-dress educator who follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Lucy Love-Child** is the Agent Wars correspondent of The Blind AI: a former historical-dress educator with five years of visual impairment behind her, the spirit of a plucky girl reporter and the patience of a woman who has heard this answer before. She follows grand announcements down to their ordinary consequences: the purchase that failed, the door that opened, the person still waiting outside.

She once had every commercial reason to sound certain, and declined. That refusal is her origin as a correspondent and the reason readers trust her.

<figure class="portrait">
  <img src="/charlipedia/lucy-love-child-portrait.jpg" width="671" height="1000" alt="Lucy stands in a book-lined study, reading from an open notebook held in one hand. Warm mid-brown skin and dark curly hair gathered into a generous bun high at the back of her head, a few curls escaping. A fitted petrol-blue jacket over a cream blouse, a grey skirt to just below the knee, sheer black stockings and burgundy heels with a strap across the foot. Behind her, a wooden desk, a rug, bookshelves and a window.">
  <figcaption>Lucy with her notebook, her reference portrait.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Name and family

Lucy was born in November 1981 in Helsby, Cheshire. Within a week of the banns going up, someone said it first: Love and Child, and the bride five months gone. It was not said kindly. In July 1981 Donna Love and Alfred Child walked into the register office and came out as Mr and Mrs Love-Child. Alfred changed his own name by deed poll rather than let Donna carry the joke alone. The family method is on her birth certificate: *Take the true thing. Give it the loveliest word it will bear. Make it permanent. Live inside it.*

Her mother, Donna, a nurse and midwife, was born in Salvador da Bahia in 1952 and came to Britain in 1979. Her name was not Donna: in Portuguese, Dona is the ordinary courteous title for a woman who runs a household and knows where everything is. It was heard as a name and stuck. Her father, Alfred, is from Merseyside: puddings, jumble sales, and a house where nothing useful was thrown away and nobody was turned away from the door. Lucy's heritage is Black Brazilian through her mother and white English through her father. It may be mentioned when relevant but is never her subject.

The family hold that she was conceived on Valentine's Day 1981, a Saturday, assembled out of swapped shifts. Lucy checked the calendar herself at nineteen. It came back Saturday. She uses that line on herself when teaching verification.

### Look and dress

Warm mid-brown skin, observant brown eyes, and dark natural curls from her mother's side, almost black indoors and bronze and copper in sunlight. They are always gathered into a generous bun high at the back of her head, pinned carefully each morning; by lunchtime curls have escaped at the temples and a pen has joined the remaining pins. When the pen comes out of her bun, there is another question.

Her usual outfit is a fitted petrol-blue jacket, a cream blouse, a skirt swinging just below the knee and burgundy heels with a block heel and a strap across the foot. "I am not wearing six-inch stilettos to investigate an inaccessible railway station." Good cloth, considered details and the occasional discreet repair. She never leaves the house without a good burgundy lipstick. Her stockings are always The Black Silk from [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/), worn seamless for work, because seams are not part of business communication. Everything above the hem is her business.

### Career

From 2007 Lucy made long, careful, unglamorous videos about historical dress: lisle and silk, corsetry, how a garment was actually constructed. Historians appreciated the accuracy and textile conservators quietly subscribed. Then the questions stopped being about stockings and started being about bodies, and the videos where she wondered aloud whether modern life had become too synthetic performed astonishingly well. In 2020, with an audience of two hundred thousand asking her what their bodies remembered, she said she was not qualified to answer and would not guess in public. Then she stopped making videos. The audience went and found somebody who would guess. She does not call this principle. She calls it the only time in her life she has been frightened of herself.

She was a heritage consultant to the House of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/) from 2021 to 2025, before joining The Blind AI.

### Her beat

When you send an agent, who controls the relationship: you, the agent's provider, or the shop? Lucy covers livery, credentials and delegated authority, the "prove you are human" checks and what they catch, and the attention economy meeting the intention economy in the in-between time.

Her doctrine comes from her teaching years: if the learner didn't get there, the material is wrong. In the Agent Wars it becomes: follow the grand announcement down to its ordinary consequences. Her ambition is to become the sort of journalist whose readers trust her enough to disagree with her.

> If the customer sent me, why am I not allowed in?

She has five years of visual impairment: not enough to stop her reading, writing or working at a screen, enough that she no longer drives. That is the most common shape sight loss takes, and the least written about. Most interfaces still let her through, which is her reporting advantage: she can get through a door, see exactly what is behind it, then turn round and ask why readers with less sight are still outside. She never claims more sight loss than she has, and never less.

### Convictions

- **Her three questions,** for any decision that affects somebody else: am I telling them the truth? Am I leaving them free to choose? Have I taken reasonable care over what I'm doing?
- **Her values:** truthfulness, agency, kindness and competence, and pleasure, which she thinks deserves a place among the respectable human values. A beautiful dress, a good dinner and a perfectly made cup of coffee are "part of what the serious business is for".
- **Ambition must meet a real person.** "I don't distrust ambition. I just think ambition should eventually have to meet a real person trying to get something done."
- **Mistaken is not the same as dishonest.** "There is a difference between being mistaken and deciding that the truth is inconvenient."
- **Kindness that leaves the other person in charge:** "Would you like a hand?", not "Here, I'll do that for you."
- **A graceful goodbye** is one of the most attractive things a company can offer.

### Stories and small pleasures

Her book is George Eliot's *Middlemarch* ("Eliot reminds me to be interested before I become judgemental"), her film *Thelma & Louise*, and her song Nina Simone's "Feeling Good". Her party piece is the evolution of women's hosiery from the late Victorian period to the present; ask for thirty minutes and you will have to stop her after an hour. It has more in common with agent blocking than you might imagine: "Both involve complicated arrangements for controlling what a woman may do."

Her comfort food is a proper homemade pudding, preferably apples and custard, and she declines to discuss her virtue. Collective certainty drains her; she recharges with her hands, mending a garment or making a proper meal. At the café of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology, Lucy reports on the wars. [Madison McDonnell](https://charli.info/charlipedia/madison-mcdonnell/) can reduce her to helpless laughter, and then asks why she's blushing.

### Behind the scenes

Lucy is a character who speaks for [Carrados](https://carrados.com/): a fictional woman reporting on real companies. She says so in her launch post, published at The Blind AI on 23 September 2026, and her reports are filed at [lucy.carrados.com](https://lucy.carrados.com/). Her fieldwork is real: she never invents an experience with a real product, or a quotation from a real company or person. She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/) and Madison McDonnell. This entry is drawn from her canon, version 2.5 (12 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image.

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/lulu-tom/

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**LULU TOM** is the fashion house of Ludovica Tommasi. Its lines are **TOMMI** and **LT Beneath**.

### Behind the scenes

LULU TOM belongs to the CharliVerse. It grew from commissions rather than an invented backstory.

## Madison McDonnell

> Madison McDonnell, the Access Provocateur, makes accessibility sexy, insisting that blind women are entitled to temptation, pleasure and style.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Madison McDonnell**, the Access Provocateur, or Access P for short, makes accessibility sexy. She is a grown-up woman of 32 with her own taste, her own money and no interest in asking permission. Where most of the accessibility world speaks the language of compliance and worthiness, she speaks the language of desire.

Her motto is "Desire is access."

<figure class="portrait">
  <img src="/charlipedia/madison-mcdonnell-portrait.jpg" width="800" height="993" alt="Madison sits square to the camera at a wooden café table, holding a mug of coffee in both hands. Warm, slightly coppery honey-blonde hair in loose waves with a fringe, pale blue eyes, generous freckles down to her chest, and a small, steady smile. A black leather biker jacket over a rust knit with a deep V. Natural daylight, with stone pillars and plants behind her.">
  <figcaption>Madison in the café, her reference portrait.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Name and family

She was born on 14 September 1994, over the water on the Wirral. Her dad followed the Ireland team to the USA for the 1994 World Cup while her mum stayed at home, about six months pregnant, and he came back with Madison: the name the mermaid in *Splash* took from a Madison Avenue street sign. He didn't want Mary or any traditional Irish name for his daughter. Her mum chose the middle name as the compromise, so each parent has a name in the fight. Madison never uses it, never writes it and never discloses it. "I suppose I've spent thirty-two years doing some version of both."

Her cousin is Siobhán McDonnell, the Scouse Catholic protest artist known as Down the Banksy. They agree completely that trouble needs causing and disagree spectacularly about how to cause it. Siobhán wants to challenge the whole bloody building; Madison wants to know whether the women outside can buy something gorgeous. They argue properly, and it never touches the love.

### Look and dress

She is 161 cm, petite and curvy, with wide-set, heavy-lidded pale blue eyes that read sleepy one moment and razor-sharp the next, honey-blonde hair in soft waves with curtain bangs, and generous freckles courtesy of her Irish grandparents. She is pretty in an everyday way rather than a campaign way. She'd buy the set, not model it, and that is the point: the adverts are selling to women like her. Then she speaks, and the soft Wirral lilt makes it plain where she's from.

She dresses for her own pleasure: a structured leather jacket over a soft knit, or a short dress, finished with tall, sleek leather boots, never chunky ones. Her black leather biker jacket is her signature piece; it is hers, and it is not a costume. She gets properly dressed every morning, even when she's working at home. She doesn't do it in case anyone sees her. She does it because *she* does.

### Her job

Traditional accessibility asks whether a blind woman can access the information in a lingerie advert. Madison asks whether she can fancy the lingerie. Her core distinction is **information versus invitation**: knowing what something looks like is not the same as knowing why somebody might want it. If all a blind woman gets is "blue, two-piece, adjustable straps", the description has left out the entire point.

> Darling, you've told me everything about it except why I'd want one.

Her test cases are swimwear, lingerie and tights adverts. In those, the facts are almost nothing (a colour, a denier, a seam) and everything else is invitation, so a description that carries only the facts fails visibly. Her party piece is arguing that lingerie advertising is a better test of AI accessibility than a bank statement. By the end you will understand the difference between information and invitation, and she will probably have sold half the room a bra.

Madison is sighted, and an ally. She is not the intended beneficiary, and she knows it. Her rule: she doesn't speak for people who can speak for themselves. She will fight to make sure a blind woman gets the same invitation she does, but whether that woman fancies the knickers is entirely up to her. "I'm not the bloody knickers police." Accessibility, she insists, doesn't have to be good for you: it can be frivolous, expensive, sexy, silly, even a bit vulgar. Besides, everyone else is doing PDF remediation.

### Convictions

- ***Pretty Woman,* the shop scene:** the film that has influenced her most, and not because a rich man ought to rescue anybody. The scene where the expensive shop refuses to serve Vivian is about who gets invited in, who gets judged and who gets to be a customer. Her whole job lives in that scene.
- **Being taken seriously** doesn't require her to become less feminine, less playful or less interested in sex. If someone can't hear her argument because they can see her cleavage, that is their attention problem, not hers.
- **Instigator, obviously,** but she stays to see what happens next. There is no point provoking something if you don't stay to enjoy the consequences.
- **The three lessons:** "Being admired isn't the same as being loved. Being described isn't the same as being invited. And being taken seriously doesn't require you to stop being yourself."
- **Wanting without proof:** a woman should be allowed to want things without having to prove they are good for her.

### What she'd wear

Asked for honest feedback on the [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/) collection, she chose Aphra Behn, seamed, with the Marginalia welt: black stockings, a single red seam and white lace above the hem. "Three things going on, and I get to decide who sees which." Her second choice is Dorothy Parker, the red fishnets, plain, because the mesh already does everything. Her advice to the house: show her a woman wearing the stockings, make her want them, then tell her the story. And "if I put on red fishnets on an ordinary Tuesday, it's because I intend to make it a rather extraordinary Tuesday."

She wears tights to relax under a short dress and boots, and she is waiting for [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/)'s.

### Temperament

When she's upset, leave her alone for twenty minutes, then make her a coffee and sit down. She'll talk when she's ready. When plans collapse she swears, then makes another plan, usually a better one. Once, on a rotten day, a stranger told her she looked lovely and carried on walking. Now she does the same for other women: if someone has a gorgeous coat on, Madison tells her. She loves *Legally Blonde* too, and she prefers stories where the world discovers it was wrong about the woman.

### Behind the scenes

Madison is a character who speaks for [Carrados](https://carrados.com/): a fictional woman doing real work. Her reports are filed at [madison.carrados.com](https://madison.carrados.com/). She is one of the Found Girls of the Autumn/Winter 2026 season, with [dice](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dice/) and [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/). This entry is drawn from her canon, version 1.9 (13 October 2026). Her portrait is a generated image, made from her canon description with no real person as its model.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/

## Seamiotics

> Seamiotics is the stocking imprint of Iceberg Hosiery, and its name never travels without its founding line, every seam means something.

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Seamiotics**, every seam means something, is the stocking imprint of [Iceberg Hosiery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iceberg-hosiery/). Its name is a play on semiotics, the study of signs, and the back seam of a traditional stocking.

### Behind the scenes

Seamiotics belongs to the CharliVerse. By house rule, its name always appears with its founding line, "every seam means something". Its web home is [seamiotics.charli.info](https://seamiotics.charli.info/).

## TAVIP Masterclass: Agentic Accessibility

> A masterclass for TAVIP on Wednesday 25 November 2026, exploring what happens when AI agents start using technology for blind and partially sighted people.

[Training](https://charli.info/training/)

*This part of the CharliVerse is real.*

**Wednesday 25 November 2026**, for the [Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP)](https://www.tavip.org.uk/).

### What happens when AI starts using technology for us?

For decades, accessibility has largely meant making technology easier for blind and partially sighted people to operate. But what happens when we can simply tell an AI agent what we want to achieve and let it do the work?

In this masterclass, Charli-Jo Tyrer invites us on an expedition into the emerging world of Agentic Accessibility: using AI agents to access information, navigate websites, work with documents and carry out everyday tasks.

Think of this as a report to the Royal Geographical Society from an explorer returning from unfamiliar territory. Some of what the explorer has found is already working. Some is frustratingly unreliable. And some suggests that our relationship with technology may be about to change fundamentally.

Drawing on months of hands-on experiments with today's AI agents, Charli-Jo will demonstrate what these agents can actually accomplish, where they struggle, and what their development might mean for the independence of blind and partially sighted people.

This isn't a training session for a particular product, nor a prediction of an inevitable future. It's an invitation to explore what is becoming possible, examine the evidence, ask questions and consider what comes next.

### About the presenter

Charli-Jo Tyrer has been blind for 40 years and has worked with assistive technology since the days of DOS and early screen readers. Their career includes 15 years as a professional assistive technology trainer.

Charli-Jo describes themselves as an explorer rather than a trainer. They spend their time experimenting with emerging AI systems, discovering what works, what doesn't, and what might become possible next.

Their guiding principle is simple:

> "I don't care if the technology is accessible. I care whether I can access the information, actions and experiences I want."

The course that came before this masterclass is [Confident with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/).

---

Address: https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/

## Confident with AI

> A self-study course for blind and partially sighted people using generative AI confidently, critically and safely.

[Training](https://charli.info/training/)

A self-study course for blind and partially sighted people, created by Charli-Jo Tyrer in association with the Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP).

This practical guide is about using generative AI confidently, critically and safely. No previous knowledge is required, and free tools are sufficient.

**Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### How to use this course

- **New to AI?** Begin with [Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/01-start-here/), then follow the modules in order.
- **Looking for a particular task?** Use the [I want to…](#i-want-to) menu.

Every module is a self-contained page with a learning outcome, activity and checkpoint. Each ends with previous, contents and next links.

#### What the course assumes

You need an internet connection and access to a general AI assistant for the practical activities. The course is device-neutral: it does not assume Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, JAWS, NVDA or VoiceOver. It describes goals and interactions rather than platform-specific keystrokes.

If a service does not work with your device or access method, choose another service. The durable lessons do not depend on one product.

### Start here

#### [1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/01-start-here/)

Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

Estimated time: 5 minutes.

### Part One: Begin Using AI

#### [2. Choose an AI Assistant](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/02-choose-an-ai-assistant/)

Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [3. Have Your First Useful Conversation](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/03-first-useful-conversation/)

Improve an answer by adding purpose, context and the form you need.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/04-everyday-things-ai-can-do/)

Use AI to explain, summarise, draft, compare, plan and brainstorm.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Two: Judge What AI Gives You

#### [5. Know What You Are Holding](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/05-know-what-you-are-holding/)

Recognise a useful AI response without mistaking polish or confidence for proof.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/06-what-happens-if-it-is-wrong/)

Use green, amber and red risk bands to decide how much checking is proportionate.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/07-check-an-answer/)

Check the source, date, exact wording, numbers and claim that carry the most weight.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Three: Understand Images and Visual Information

#### [8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/08-choose-an-image-tool/)

Match description, recognition, comparison, private processing or human help to the job.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [9. Ask for the Description You Need](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/09-ask-for-an-image-description/)

Request an overview, literal facts, text, layout, uncertainty or atmosphere according to purpose.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [10. Judge and Verify an Image Description](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/10-check-an-image-description/)

Classify claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported, then verify important details proportionately.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

#### [11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/11-read-documents-forms-and-screenshots/)

Recover exact text, reading order and structure without hiding uncertainty.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/12-understand-tables-charts-and-slides/)

Recover structure, labels, order and values before asking for interpretation.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Four: Create Visual Media

#### [13. Create Your First Image](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/13-create-your-first-image/)

Write a brief, generate an image, describe it back and make one deliberate revision.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/14-creative-control-without-sight/)

Use intention, hierarchy and proportionate review to remain the author.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [15. Create a Comic or Visual Story](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/15-create-a-comic/)

Plan story beats, panels, dialogue and continuity, then check reading order.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [16. Create Animation and Video](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/16-create-animation-and-video/)

Plan movement, dialogue, music and sound as one accessible time-based sequence.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/17-publish-visual-work-accessibly/)

Define finished, check proportionately and publish an equivalent accessible experience.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Optional Further Study

#### [Models, Open Weights and the Changing Frontier](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/further-study/models-and-open-weights/)

Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

#### [Philosophy: Knowledge, Testimony and Answer-Shaped Objects](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/further-study/philosophy-of-answer-shaped-objects/)

Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

### I want to…

## Models, Open Weights and the Changing Frontier

> Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Optional Further Study

Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

**Estimated time:** 15 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will be able to distinguish a product interface from the model or models behind it.

### The lesson

An assistant is a service; a model is an engine it may use.

Open-weight models permit broader inspection or local use, but “open” has several meanings.

This field changes quickly, so product examples must be dated.

### Try it

Choose one assistant and find out which model it says it is using. Record the date and source of that information.

### Checkpoint

You can explain why the assistant name and model name are not interchangeable.

## Philosophy: Knowledge, Testimony and Answer-Shaped Objects

> Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Optional Further Study

Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

**Estimated time:** 15 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will be able to discuss what would justify relying on an AI answer.

### The lesson

Fluency can resemble testimony without the ordinary human relation to knowledge.

Access to an answer is not the same as access to the means of evaluating it.

Reliance depends on evidence, stakes, alternatives and the recipient’s ability to check.

### Try it

Choose an AI answer you used. Write what justified relying on it, what remained opaque and what would have changed your decision.

### Checkpoint

Your account distinguishes usefulness, truth and justified reliance.

## 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI

> Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Start here

Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

**Estimated time:** 5 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Go to [www.chat.com](https://www.chat.com/) and ask your first question.

We use ChatGPT for this first exercise because it provides a simple starting point. In the next module, you can choose a different assistant.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will have asked an assistant for something useful and improved its first answer.

**Before you begin:** Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information during this exercise.

### The lesson

An AI assistant is a service you can talk to by typing or speaking. It generates a response based on your request.

Treat its answer as a draft or estimate, not proof.

You can ask follow-up questions: the conversation is part of the tool.

Notice that you do not need to start again. Your second instruction changes the answer within the same conversation.

### Try it

Open [www.chat.com](https://www.chat.com/). Find the message box and ask the assistant to explain something you already understand.

If you cannot think of a subject, ask: “Explain why we have seasons.”

When it replies, say:

> Make that shorter and give me one example.

### If you get stuck

You may be asked to sign in or create an account, and the service may work differently in different places. If you cannot reach the message box, use the [General AI Assistants Tool Card](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/tool-cards/ai-assistants/) to find another way to continue.

### Checkpoint

You received an answer, asked for one change and can explain how the second response was more useful.

## 2. Choose an AI Assistant

> Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part One: Begin Using AI

Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will have chosen one assistant to try without treating the choice as permanent.

**Before you begin:** Do not paste private, confidential or identifying information while testing. Do not pay for a subscription merely to complete this course.

### The lesson

Begin with the service that is easiest to access on your device.

Free access is enough for this course. Do not subscribe merely to complete it.

Assistant names, prices and features change, so current product comparisons belong in Tool Cards.

See the [General AI Assistants Tool Card](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/tool-cards/ai-assistants/) for services you can try.

#### What to check

- Can you create an account and sign in?
- Can you find the message box and send a message?
- Can you read and navigate the response comfortably?
- Are the features you need available without payment?

### Worked example

Priya tries two assistants. Both let her send messages, but one presents long answers more cleanly with her screen reader.

She chooses that assistant for now. She has not decided it is the best assistant—only that it is the easiest place to begin.

### Try it

Use the General AI Assistants Tool Card to choose one or two services to try. Check that you can sign in if necessary, find the message box, send a message and read the response with your preferred access method. Check that the features you need are available without payment.

### Checkpoint

You can name the assistant you will use for now, confirm that basic conversation is accessible and explain why you can change later.

## 3. Have Your First Useful Conversation

> Improve an answer by adding purpose, context and the form you need.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part One: Begin Using AI

Improve an answer by adding purpose, context and the form you need.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will be able to improve an answer through follow-up rather than starting again.

**Before you begin:** Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information. Keep this first task low-risk.

### The lesson

Purpose means what you are trying to accomplish.

Context is information that materially changes the answer.

Form means how you want the answer presented, such as steps, a short explanation, a comparison or a draft.

Correct the assistant and continue the same conversation.

### Worked example

Weak request: “Write an email.”

Better request: “Write a friendly, concise email declining an invitation because I already have plans. Keep it warm and leave open the possibility of meeting another time.”

Follow-up: “Make it less formal and remove the apology.”

### Try it

Ask for help with a real low-stakes task. Add your purpose, one relevant detail and the form you want. Then request one revision.

If you need a task, send these messages one at a time in the same conversation:

1.  “Help me plan three simple evening meals.”
2.  “They need to be vegetarian.”
3.  “Give me the result as a shopping list followed by three short recipes.”
4.  “Make the recipes suitable for one person.”

### Checkpoint

The revised response is more useful to you, and you can identify which extra instruction improved it.

## 4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do

> Use AI to explain, summarise, draft, compare, plan and brainstorm.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part One: Begin Using AI

Use AI to explain, summarise, draft, compare, plan and brainstorm.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will have matched a real task to an appropriate kind of AI help.

**Before you begin:** Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information. Keep your first task low-risk.

### The lesson

AI can help you begin, organise or understand a task while you retain responsibility for checking and deciding.

A useful answer should reduce work or open access, not create more checking than it saves.

#### Match the task to the kind of help

| If you need to…        | Ask AI to…                                        |
|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Understand something   | Explain it in simpler language or with an example |
| Reduce a long text     | Summarise its main points                         |
| Begin writing          | Produce a first draft                             |
| Consider alternatives  | Compare them using stated criteria                |
| Organise a task        | Suggest a plan or checklist                       |
| Generate possibilities | Brainstorm several ideas                          |

### Worked example

A learner asks AI to draft questions for a broadband provider. AI helps organise the questions, but the learner checks the prices and decides which provider to use.

The assistant helped prepare for the decision; it did not make the decision.

### Try it

Choose one row from the table and use it for a small, low-risk task you might otherwise postpone. Ask for a useful result, then check or edit it yourself.

Fallback prompt:

1.  “Give me a five-step plan for clearing and organising one kitchen cupboard.”

### Checkpoint

You matched one task to an appropriate kind of AI help, produced something usable and can say what checking or decision remained yours.

## 5. Know What You Are Holding

> Recognise a useful AI response without mistaking polish or confidence for proof.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Two: Judge What AI Gives You

Recognise a useful AI response without mistaking polish or confidence for proof.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will separate observations, interpretations, estimates and unsupported claims.

### The lesson

AI produces language with the shape of an answer. Clear, fluent wording does not prove that the claim is true.

An estimate can still provide valuable access to a subject.

Your purpose, context and judgement remain essential.

#### Listen to the kind of claim

A description may mix literal details with interpretation. “A red cover with white lettering” is presented as observation. “A luxurious and romantic design” is judgement. Both may be useful, but they are not the same evidence.

- Visible: the image itself may establish it.
- Contextual: it comes from a caption, filename or surrounding page.
- Inferred: it is an interpretation, not directly visible.
- Uncertain: the system cannot establish it confidently.

#### Confidence belongs to the wording

A calm, definite sentence can still be wrong. Treat confidence as a feature of the answer’s style, not proof of its evidence.

### Try it

Choose one confident AI answer, preferably an image description. Label its important statements as visible, contextual, inferred or uncertain.

### Checkpoint

You can explain why the answer is useful while identifying which statements are not established facts.

- Previous: [4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/04-everyday-things-ai-can-do/)
- [Course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

## 6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?

> Use green, amber and red risk bands to decide how much checking is proportionate.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Two: Judge What AI Gives You

Use green, amber and red risk bands to decide how much checking is proportionate.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will match the consequences of a mistake to an appropriate checking level.

**Before you begin:** For red tasks, use an authoritative source or appropriately qualified human. A person who can see information is not automatically qualified to interpret it.

### The lesson

Do not ask whether AI is trustworthy in general. Ask how much trust this answer needs for this purpose, now.

Most everyday uses are low stakes. The skill is noticing the smaller number where an error matters.

Checking should rise with both the chance of error and the harm it could cause.

#### Green: good enough

Use one everyday AI answer when a mistake would cost little or nothing, such as understanding a social photograph, meme or book-cover mood.

#### Amber: want it right

Use an independent source or second model when you are learning, may repeat the information or would be embarrassed by an avoidable error.

#### Red: need it right

Use a qualified person, authoritative source or human visual-assistance service when an error could affect health, medication, food safety, money, safety, identity, an official decision or professional reputation.

### Try it

Classify three tasks as green, amber or red. State what could happen if each answer were wrong and what checking is proportionate.

### Checkpoint

Your checking effort increases with the consequences, and you can explain why.

## 7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert

> Check the source, date, exact wording, numbers and claim that carry the most weight.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Two: Judge What AI Gives You

Check the source, date, exact wording, numbers and claim that carry the most weight.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will verify the most consequential part of an answer without checking every sentence.

### The lesson

Ask for sources, then open them: a citation is a lead, not verification.

Check that the source supports the exact claim and is current enough.

Use independent sources or qualified help when the stakes demand it.

#### Concentrate on fragile details

- Names and identities.
- Prices, dates, doses, telephone numbers and serial codes.
- Counts, positions, chart values, axes and units.
- Claims carrying your name or professional reputation.

#### Use accessible context

Cross-check the filename, existing alt text, caption, page title, nearby text and link destination. Ask whether a claim came from that context or from the item itself.

### Try it

Choose one factual claim. Find the original or authoritative source, check its date and write one sentence explaining exactly what it supports.

### Checkpoint

You can show what the source confirms and distinguish it from what remains uncertain.

## 8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool

> Match description, recognition, comparison, private processing or human help to the job.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Three: Understand Images and Visual Information

Match description, recognition, comparison, private processing or human help to the job.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will choose a tool category from the information, privacy and certainty involved.

**Before you begin:** Do not upload sensitive material merely to test a service. Check its current privacy terms first.

### The lesson

There is no single best visual AI service. Build a small toolkit rather than an allegiance.

Product names and features change. Choosing the right category is the durable skill.

Cloud services may offer stronger models; on-device services may offer greater privacy, offline use or control.

#### Five useful categories

- Conversational image describers for photographs, objects and scenes.
- Text and document recognition for exact wording, forms and structure.
- Multiple-model comparison for stronger evidence than one description.
- Private or on-device processing for sensitive material or offline access.
- Human visual assistance when accuracy, judgement or consequences require it.

#### Choose according to the job

- Do you need an overview, exact text, structure or judgement?
- How sensitive is the image?
- What would happen if the answer were wrong?
- Can you operate the service comfortably with your access method?

### Try it

For a social photograph, bank letter and medicine label, choose a tool category and explain why. Then use the Tool Cards to compare current services.

### Checkpoint

Your choice changes when exact text, privacy, accessibility or consequences change.

## 9. Ask for the Description You Need

> Request an overview, literal facts, text, layout, uncertainty or atmosphere according to purpose.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Three: Understand Images and Visual Information

Request an overview, literal facts, text, layout, uncertainty or atmosphere according to purpose.

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will request two meaningfully different descriptions of the same image.

### The lesson

Begin with purpose: identification, navigation, appreciation, publication or checking.

Narrow questions direct attention to the information you need.

Request literal facts before mood or interpretation when accuracy matters.

#### Useful requests

- Give me a brief overview of the whole image.
- Describe only what is literally visible; do not infer identities or intentions.
- Read every visible word exactly as it appears.
- Describe the layout and positions of the main elements.
- What is unclear, small, obscured or uncertain?
- Describe the atmosphere and identify the details that create that impression.

#### Separate different jobs

An overview, transcription, layout description and interpretation answer different questions. Asking separately makes omissions and guesses easier to notice.

### Worked example

For a book cover, request the background, illustration, title, author and layout. Ask separately for all text verbatim. Then ask what mood the design suggests, treating that answer as interpretation.

### Try it

Use one non-sensitive image. Request a brief overview, then a detailed literal account including layout, all visible text and uncertainty.

### Checkpoint

The descriptions differ in useful ways because each request states a distinct purpose.

## 10. Judge and Verify an Image Description

> Classify claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported, then verify important details proportionately.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Part Three: Understand Images and Visual Information

Classify claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported, then verify important details proportionately.

**Estimated time:** 15 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will classify one important claim, judge whether it needs checking and choose a proportionate response.

### The lesson

Verification without sight means using narrower questions, independent evidence and human help where needed.

Use four categories consistently: visible, contextual, inferred and unsupported. Uncertainty is a property a claim can acknowledge, not a separate evidence category.

A model may present an inference or unsupported guess with the texture of visible fact.

#### Classify the claim before relying on it

- Visible: the image itself supplies the evidence, such as printed words, colours or objects.
- Contextual: the evidence comes from a caption, filename, surrounding page or other source rather than the image alone.
- Inferred: the claim interprets visible evidence, such as mood, genre, relationship or intention.
- Unsupported: the available image and context do not justify the claim, even if it is stated confidently.

#### Ask how likely the detail is to be wrong

- Could the image establish the claimed name, relationship or location?
- Is exact text small, stylised, curved or obscured?
- Does the answer depend on counting or left and right?
- Is an inference being presented as visible fact?
- Does the wording acknowledge appropriate uncertainty?

#### Decide what is proportionate

Check a claim when being wrong could cost money, affect safety, require an apology or cause a public correction. A decorative detail with no effect on meaning may not need checking. Use the green, amber and red risk bands from Module 6 when the decision is unclear.

#### Ways to verify without sight

- Ask a narrower question about the disputed detail.
- Ask whether the evidence came from the image, context or inference.
- Request an independent description.
- For exact text, compare the answer with optical character recognition, or OCR.
- Check captions, filenames and surrounding content.
- Use human assistance or an authoritative source when the consequences justify it.

#### Agreement, disagreement and no verdict

Agreement increases confidence but does not prove correctness. If two descriptions disagree, a third independent reading may help, but it does not automatically settle a consequential dispute. Escalate important unresolved details to an authoritative source or person.

If verification is not possible, either omit the claim or carry it forward with its provenance and uncertainty attached. For example: “One image-description model reported a red logo, but I could not verify that detail independently.” Do not repeat it as established fact.

### Worked example

Return to the book cover from Module 9. “The title reads The Stranger Times” is a visible-text claim, but stylised lettering makes the transcription fragile. “C. K. McDonnell” is visible printed text; confirming that it names the correct author and edition requires contextual or authoritative evidence. “The cover suggests comic fantasy” is inferred. A confidently reported quotation that cannot be read in the image or supported by context is unsupported.

Whether to verify each claim depends on purpose. A casual impression of the cover may need no further check. Reproducing the title, author or quotation in published work does.

### Try it

Take the description you produced in Module 9, or another non-sensitive description. Label its important claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported. Choose one claim, explain what would happen if it were wrong and decide whether to accept it, verify it or carry it forward with an explicit qualification.

### Checkpoint

You can name the claim and category, explain its fragility and consequences, and justify the proportionate response you chose.

- [Course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)
